claims.text: At ambient temperature, wear resistance of the HEA coating is primarily governed by high yield strength and strain-hardening capacity.
High yield strength and strain hardening suppress plastic deformation and abrasive plowing.
Sliding produces a protective, work-hardened surface tribolayer.
The work-hardened tribolayer reduces the coefficient of friction.
The work-hardened tribolayer prevents severe adhesive wear.
Exceeding the coating yield strength with contact stress causes catastrophic plastic flow and delamination.
A contact pressure greater than approximately 1.5 times the coating yield strength is the critical boundary for severe performance degradation.
Above the proposed boundary, the protective tribofilm cannot reform quickly enough to prevent substrate exposure.
The unspecified HEA coating is likely to have an FCC or BCC structure depending on composition.
The deposited coating has a fine-grained or nanocrystalline microstructure and a high dislocation density caused by deposition stresses.
At 20–25 °C, thermal activation is insufficient to drive dynamic recovery or recrystallization.
Severe lattice distortion and slow diffusion in HEAs impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion gives HEAs high yield strength and high strain-hardening rates.
High fracture toughness associated with the complex chemical environment suppresses crack propagation.
At ambient temperature, the HEA coating will have a lower specific wear rate than pure Ti, pure Ni, or other conventional transition-metal coatings.
Wear rate increases nonlinearly with contact pressure and undergoes a sharp transition to severe delamination near 1.5 times the coating yield strength.
Conventional TiN, CrN, or pure Ni coatings typically have ambient-temperature wear rates of 10^-5 to 10^-4 mm^3/N·m under moderate loads.
The coating phase constitution, residual stress, counterface hardness, and counterface roughness influence the yield-controlled wear boundary.
